run.question: I have a slow query on the 'app-191-profile' index. Use the profile option to analyze this query and tell me the query type used: {"wildcard": {"message": "*timeout*"}}

report.summary: I profiled the supplied query on index app-191-profile (single open index, health green, 6 documents, 5.8kb, 1 shard) using the profile option. The query type that executes is a multi-term constant-score query: the wildcard clause is profiled as a node of type MultiTermQueryConstantScoreBlendedWrapper with description "message:*timeout*", nested inside a BooleanQuery inside a ConstantScoreQuery, combined with an IndexOrDocValuesQuery for the mandatory timestamp range. That is the classic shape of an unanchored/leading wildcard: it is not a plain TermQuery lookup and cannot use a single term lookup, it is resolved through the field's term dictionary. A separate TermQuery node with description "message:timeout" is also visible in the same shard's search profile in both runs. Both profiled runs matched exactly 3 documents and, in these samples, were fast (took 18 ms and 3 ms; query-phase multi-term wrapper 231,824 ns and 179,604 ns, dominated by build_scorer 225,194 ns and 172,894 ns) on this 6-document index, so the reported slowness was not reproduced by these two profile calls. No Kubernetes, Prometheus or trace signal was needed or checked for this question, and no root-cause Kubernetes object applies.

claims.text: The index named in the question exists exactly as 'app-191-profile': health green, status open, docs.count 6, store.size 5.8kb (single shard 0, as shown by the profile).
The mappings of app-191-profile are message: text, status: keyword, timestamp: date; @timestamp is not mapped, so the timestamp field must be given as time_field for any time-filtered search.

With profile enabled (size=5), shard [yxF_y55zS0q2BKHN3zahxw][app-191-profile][0] profiles the wildcard clause as type MultiTermQueryConstantScoreBlendedWrapper with description "message:*timeout*" (time_in_nanos 231824, build_scorer 225194), nested under a node of type BooleanQuery inside a node of type ConstantScoreQuery, whose sibling clause is IndexOrDocValuesQuery(indexQuery=timestamp:[1795452895000 TO 1795456495999], dvQuery=...) — i.e. the wildcard executes as a multi-term constant-score query, not as a single-term TermQuery.

A second profile run of the same query (size=0) reproduced the identical query-type structure for the wildcard: MultiTermQueryConstantScoreBlendedWrapper "message:*timeout*" (time_in_nanos 179604, build_scorer 172894) under BooleanQuery under ConstantScoreQuery with the timestamp IndexOrDocValuesQuery; that run returned total 3 with took 3 ms.

In both profiled searches the same shard's search profile also contains a separate node of type TermQuery with description "message:timeout" (time_in_nanos 28691 in the size=5 run, 21739 in the size=0 run), distinct from the MultiTermQueryConstantScoreBlendedWrapper node built for the wildcard.

The profiled query matched exactly 3 documents (total.relation eq, value 3) in both runs; the returned documents are status=error entries with message values "Socket timeout during file upload" (timestamp 2026-11-23T17:53:00Z), "Database query timeout exceeded limit" (17:51:00Z) and "Request timeout after 30 seconds" (17:49:00Z).

In these two profiled samples the query was not slow: took was 18 ms (size=5 run, query phase 134291 ns, all clauses summed well below a millisecond of CPU in the query phase) and 3 ms (size=0 run) on this 6-document, 1-shard index.

The cost shape is consistent with the leading-wildcard pattern "*timeout*" on the analyzed text field message being resolved by iterating the field's term dictionary: the profile attributes the largest single build_scorer cost (172894-225194 ns) to the MultiTermQueryConstantScoreBlendedWrapper clause, i.e. the wildcard clause rather than the plain timestamp range (49480-68160 ns build_scorer). This is an explanation of the observed profile shape, not a measurement of slow behaviour at larger scale.

Because the profile shows the wildcard being executed as a multi-term constant-score query over the term dictionary, replacing leading-wildcard matching with a term/match query on a keyword sub-field (or indexing a normalized token such as a 'timeout' keyword and filtering on it), and keeping the timestamp range filter, would give a single-term lookup instead of a term-dictionary scan; re-run with profile on the real data volume to confirm the gain, since the two samples here took 18 ms and 3 ms.

gaps: The first elasticsearch_search call without time_field was rejected with INVALID_PARAMS TIME_FIELD_REQUIRED (query profile not produced by that call); the profiles cited come from the two subsequent calls that set time_field=timestamp.

The index holds only 6 documents in a single shard, so these profile samples cannot show the query's cost at production data volume; no slow-query log or longer-term 'took' baseline was available, and slowness was therefore not reproduced.
The profile does not explain why a separate TermQuery 'message:timeout' node also appears in the same shard's search profile; the evidence does not show which component issued it.
Elasticsearch field analyzers/normalizers were not readable beyond the type mapping (message: text), so the exact effect of analysis on wildcard term iteration could not be verified.
Change history is not an integrated source in this Run, so no configuration or index-setting change can be checked.
No Kubernetes, Prometheus or trace checks were run, as the question concerns an Elasticsearch query profile; whether this query slowness is tied to any service-level incident is unchecked.
next_steps: Capture the actual slow-query log entry (took, index, shard count, hits) for the slow execution and re-run the profile at the time and data volume where the slowness is seen.
Test the same filter as a term query on a keyword representation of the message field and compare profiled build_scorer and took values.
Inspect the index's analyzer settings and any keyword sub-field for message before changing the query, to confirm which field a fast replacement query should target.
